name: Croton
lesson_scope: Morphology-first comparison of six canonical learner species. Genus lesson enrichment only: preserve all existing species, image attributions, source decisions, range HOLDs, and taxonomy concepts. No new species added.

project_scope.species_count_note: All six already occur in data/manifest.json; installed does not imply certified target-zone native.

range_labels.croton-lindheimeri: UNRESOLVED (only Travis locked; approved learner comparison)
range_labels.croton-capitatus: UNRESOLVED TAXON CONCEPT (no locked target-zone county count; approved learner comparison)

shared_genus_pattern.look_here_first: Inspect the lower leaf surface with magnification for stellate (star-shaped) or scalelike hairs, then find a pistillate flower or capsule. On a flowering plant, check if male and female flowers share the same plant, the number/division of styles, pistillate sepal posture and whether capsules are smooth or warty.
shared_genus_pattern.vegetative: Herbs through shrubs, usually alternate simple leaves; leaf outlines vary widely. Stellate or lepidote hairs are an important Croton clue. Gray-looking leaves alone do not make a species ID.
shared_genus_pattern.reproductive: Flowers generally small and unisexual, often with lower pistillate and upper staminate flowers along mixed inflorescences in monoecious species. Dioecious species have male and female flowers on separate plants.
shared_genus_pattern.fruit: Usually a three-part capsule in the current group; prairie tea is exceptional: two locules with only one fertile, yielding an apparently one-seeded, follicle-like fruit.
shared_genus_pattern.family_tie_breaker: Against Euphorbia, look for Croton's stellate/scalelike hairs and ordinary separate tiny unisexual flowers rather than cyathia. Against Acalypha, inspect reproductive spikes and the characteristic Acalypha pistillate bracts rather than relying on leaf outline.

central_texas_look_here_first: ONE: Identify a WOODY basal stem versus an annual. Shrubby C. fruticulosus should have woody basal growth + minutely serrulate leaves, not merely a leafy green tip.
TWO: A narrow-leaved annual with SEPARATE male/female plants and warted fruit likely C. texensis; male stamens in existing photos do NOT prove female fruit.
THREE: Low branchy annuals → FLIP LEAF, 10–20×: DARK-CENTERED stellate hair underside + 2 forked styles/FOUR tips = C. monanthogynus.
FOUR: Low branchy annual WITHOUT brown-centered hairs + 3 forked styles/SIX tips = C. lindheimerianus. Do not count any visible male stamens as female style ends.
FIVE: Tall woolly annuals → use mature female sepal tips and acute/blunt leaf tips to separate C. lindheimeri from TRUE C. capitatus, maintaining both existing range/taxon HOLDs.

comparison_matrix.monanthogynus: Small annual; often many branches near base.
comparison_matrix.lindheimerianus: Small annual; often dichotomous branching near base.
comparison_matrix.texensis: Annual; loosely branching toward upper stem.
comparison_matrix.lindheimeri: Larger annual, commonly with stronger upright main axis.
comparison_matrix.capitatus: Woolly annual, variable; habit alone insufficient.

comparison_matrix.texensis: Dioecious; separate male and female plants.

comparison_matrix.lindheimerianus: Entire; variable lanceolate to almost round.
comparison_matrix.capitatus: Entire; some leaves obtuse or mucronate.

comparison_matrix.monanthogynus: Some stellate hairs DARK-CENTERED, creating brown-dot effect abaxially.
comparison_matrix.lindheimerianus: Stellate hairs without brown dot effect.
comparison_matrix.fruticulosus: Stellate hairs; inspect woody stems and serrulation.
comparison_matrix.lindheimeri: Ochraceous yellow-brown woolly hairs on young growth; no brown-dot effect.
comparison_matrix.capitatus: Pale whitish to yellowish stellate wool; no brown-dot effect.

comparison_matrix.monanthogynus: Two styles, each bifid: FOUR terminal segments.
comparison_matrix.lindheimerianus: Three styles, each bifid: SIX terminal segments.
comparison_matrix.texensis: Three strongly multifid styles: 12–32+ terminal segments.
comparison_matrix.fruticulosus: Three bifid styles: SIX terminal segments.
comparison_matrix.lindheimeri: Three repeatedly forked styles: typically TWELVE terminal segments.
comparison_matrix.capitatus: Three repeatedly forked styles: typically 12–18 or more terminal segments.

comparison_matrix.monanthogynus: Five relatively short sepals; essentially one-seeded smooth capsule.
comparison_matrix.lindheimerianus: Five to six short sepals, about 3 mm; smooth three-locular capsule.
comparison_matrix.fruticulosus: Five short sepals, about 2.2 mm; smooth capsule.
comparison_matrix.lindheimeri: Seven to eight woolly sepals about 5–7 mm; tips straight or slightly incurved, not recurved.
comparison_matrix.capitatus: Six to nine long persistent sepals, often 7–10 mm or longer in fruit, tips flaring or recurved outward.

comparison_matrix.monanthogynus: PASS; brown-dot hairs + four style tips strongest.
comparison_matrix.lindheimerianus: PASS; distinguish from C. monanthogynus by underside and style count.
comparison_matrix.texensis: PASS; sex system and warty fruit first.
comparison_matrix.fruticulosus: PASS; woody base and leaf serrulation first.
comparison_matrix.lindheimeri: RANGE UNRESOLVED; not counted native; old C. capitatus var. lindheimeri resolves here.
comparison_matrix.capitatus: TAXON-CONCEPT UNRESOLVED locally; older C. capitatus var. lindheimeri records DO NOT certify true C. capitatus.

head_to_head.split: Prairie tea: dark-centered stars look brown-dotted, two bifid styles/four tips, effectively one seed. Lindheimer's croton: no brown dots, three bifid styles/six tips, three-locular capsule.
head_to_head.sterile_caution: If a leaf underside is too small to resolve with a field lens and no female flowers/fruit are present, leave the species tentative.

head_to_head.look_here_first: Brown-dot hairs versus dioecious flowers / warty fruit.
head_to_head.split: Prairie tea monoecious with one-seeded smooth fruit; Texas croton dioecious with narrow leaves and wart-covered three-part capsules.
head_to_head.sterile_caution: A lone male Texas croton plant cannot establish dioecy by itself; seek a female plant or fruit before asserting the distinction.

head_to_head.look_here_first: Female sepals on mature inflorescences, backed by leaf tips and young-stem color.
head_to_head.split: C. lindheimeri has more ochraceous young wool, mostly acute leaf apices, and straight to slightly incurved sepals; true C. capitatus more often has some blunt/mucronate leaves and long sepals recurving outward after anthesis.
head_to_head.sterile_caution: Historical 'C. capitatus var. lindheimeri' belongs with C. lindheimeri; do not show a mislabeled historical voucher as proof of true C. capitatus. Both scientific statuses stay unresolved for target-zone metrics.

head_to_head.look_here_first: Stem base and teeth along leaf margin, then sex system/fruit.
head_to_head.split: C. fruticulosus has woody stems, finely serrulate foliage, and bisexual racemes on one plant. C. texensis is an herbaceous dioecious annual with largely entire narrow leaves and warty fruit.
head_to_head.sterile_caution: Photograph the basal woody portion; a shoot-tip closeup does not prove shrub versus annual.

head_to_head.look_here_first: Female sepal length and style branching.
head_to_head.split: C. lindheimerianus has short pistillate sepals (~3 mm) and styles with six ultimate tips; C. lindheimeri has longer woolly sepals (~5–7 mm) and repeatedly forked styles, often twelve ultimate tips.
head_to_head.sterile_caution: Leaf fuzz alone can overlap; use a magnified female flower.

photo_requirements.detail: Same-magnification close-ups, one with dark brown-centered stellate trichomes and one lacking dark centers; annotate actual trichomes with arrows, not random leaf texture.
Full-focus front/oblique close-ups showing 2 bifid styles/4 tips versus 3 bifid styles/6 tips; arrows point to style branches.
Same developmental stage, side-on angle, with scale: sepals straight/incurved versus outward flaring/recurved; taxonomy and exact ID must be independently confirmed.

photo_requirements.role: Female warty capsule plus male/female whole inflorescences
photo_requirements.detail: Close-up in focus on verrucose fruit; separate correctly sexed plant photos.

photo_requirements.role: Woody basal stem and serrulate leaf edge
photo_requirements.detail: Two precise diagnostic photos rather than merely another upper-shoot view. Two CC0 structural photos were added for female flower and underside hairs, but neither substitutes for ground-level woody crown and actual edge serrulation.
Mature fruit with size reference and true microscopic/hair close-up.

photo_requirements.role: Three-part smooth capsule and 6 style tips
photo_requirements.detail: Separate macro of both structures, ideally with ruler or metric scale.
Current NC State public-domain exact species photo is physically installed, but does not confirm full mature outward-recurving pistillate sepals; local taxon concept still unresolved.

visual_comparison.title: Six Crotons — actual hair, reproductive and leaf photos with explicit missing diagnostic views
visual_comparison.subtitle: Eleven genus photo panels including two physically installed shrubby croton CC0 macros; arrows point only to visible parts. Female sepal posture for woolly pair and woody base / leaf teeth still need exact photographic proofs.
visual_comparison.memory_rule: BROWN-DOT HAIR + FOUR style tips = prairie tea. NO brown dots + SIX tips = three-seed. Narrow dioecious + WARTY fruit = Texas Croton. WOODY + minute leaf teeth = shrubby. Woolly pair: compare mature FEMALE sepal posture, not wool color alone.

items.label: 1 · Prairie tea — low branching plant
items.creator: Krzysztof Ziarnek, Kenraiz
items.image_role: Source-correct real prairie tea whole plant, NOT dark-centered stellate-hair microscope
items.caption: A low annual branches repeatedly, carrying numerous pale small leaves and minute cream flower clusters. The brown-dotted underside and precisely four style tips are NOT visible at this scale.
items.why_it_matters: Teaches prairie tea's branching silhouette, which can overlap C. lindheimerianus; do not identify on shape alone.

items.label: 2 · Prairie tea — Glass Root Garden leafy stems
items.creator: Glass Root Garden
items.image_role: Owner's exact-source greenery and developing inflorescences, star hair centers unresolvable
items.caption: Owner photo shows alternating short-stalked leaves of variable size along slender branches and small clusters of greenish flowers. The leaf underside texture is NOT magnified enough to prove a brown-centered star hair.
items.why_it_matters: Good real-world look of the stem-leaf architecture in local-style mixed growth.

items.label: 3 · Prairie tea — Glass Root Garden full low habit
items.creator: Glass Root Garden
items.image_role: Owner's true source specimen full annual bushy habit on rocky ground
items.caption: The plant occupies a low rounded mound of many short densely leafy branches; flowers are tiny. The photographed base is partly hidden and no individual stellate-hair centers or female style branches can be counted.
items.why_it_matters: Crew first-recognition photo, not a diagnostic specimen at microscale.

items.label: 1 · Three-seed croton — Joey's flower & leaf macro
items.creator: Joey Santore
items.image_role: Real source-correct flower branch and densely hairy broad leaves; separate 6 styles not visible
items.caption: The broad leaf's pale star-hair texture, hairy stem, several small rounded buds/developing flowers and a WHITE STAMINATE flower with projecting stamens are visible. DO NOT label the nearby pale protrusions as six countable female style tips; they are overlapping.
items.why_it_matters: Shows micro-hair coverage and small sexual flower structures. Hair centers and true style count require greater resolution and right angle.

items.label: 2 · Three-seed croton — Joey's flowering nodes
items.creator: Joey Santore
items.image_role: Real source-correct paired-looking leaf cluster from SHORT close internodes, tiny clustered flowers and fuzzy axis
items.caption: Pale furry leaves crowd close to tiny pistillate/staminate flower structures. One green left leaf and one green right leaf can LOOK opposite because crowded at a branch node; Croton leaves are normally ALTERNATE. Neither star-hair dark centers nor six style-tip branches can be reliably counted here.
items.why_it_matters: Shows how crowded Croton inflorescence leaves can fool a novice into calling leaf arrangement opposite.

items.label: TEXAS CROTON — actual male staminate flowers
items.creator: Joey Santore
items.image_role: Exact-taxon MALE staminate flowers; female wart-covered capsule not shown
items.caption: White flowers with many projecting stamens on a hairy branching MALE C. texensis shoot. The diagnostic WARTY FEMALE capsule and separate female plant are NOT pictured. A male-only stem cannot independently demonstrate dioecy.

items.label: SHRUBBY CROTON — leafy stem and actual flowers
items.creator: Glass Root Garden
items.image_role: Exact-taxon leafy branches, individual female/male small flowers, not the woody crown or microleaf teeth
items.caption: Actual Glass Root Garden Croton fruticulosus branch in rocky terrain. Simple elliptic-ovate leaves and little whitish flowers show well; basal WOODY crown and very fine leaf-margin SERRULATIONS are not resolvable at this scale.

items.image_role: Licensed source-identified TRUE Croton capitatus specimen showing male stamens, woolly bracts; DOES NOT prove mature recurved female sepal tips and not certified Hays

items.image_role: Real CC BY source-credited remote image, NOT a confirmed diagnostic mature-female-sepal macro

items.creator: Gaiacoyote

items.caption: Actual Gaiacoyote CC0 macro showing a female Croton fruticulosus flower. Two new arrows aim at the visible curved style tissue and female flower body. The image should NOT be used to assert all SIX terminal style tips are individually countable; not a woody-base or margin-tooth proof.

study_cautions: Most Croton leaves are alternate, yet leaves crowd near some inflorescences; do not call the apparent leaf clusters a reliable opposite-leaf arrangement.
Look at pistillate (female) flowers to count the style branches; a male-only stem cannot show them.
The terms 'goatweed', 'doveweed' and 'croton' are reused across species and are not diagnostic.
Brown-dotted underside refers to dark centers in star-shaped hairs, not disease or reddish glands.
Croton capitatus and Croton lindheimeri historical synonymy is a real trap; never silently merge or count them both from the same old voucher.
Installed learner taxa do not all meet the three-county native certification criterion; do not convert two unresolved records into target-native PASS.
Existing images are provisional faces; do not label these as diagnostic micrographs when the key trait is not visibly resolved.

genus_diagnostics.hair_character: Stellate (star-shaped) or scale-like hairs on at least some foliage or stems; check a true hair structure with a hand lens.
genus_diagnostics.leaves: Simple mostly alternate leaves; margins and habit vary across species.
genus_diagnostics.flowers: Small unisexual flowers; pistillate and staminate parts on one monoecious plant or on separate dioecious plants, depending on species.
genus_diagnostics.female_parts: Female styles and their branching are a particularly strong species-level character: 4 versus 6 versus many terminal arms.
genus_diagnostics.fruits: Usually a three-part capsule; C. monanthogynus is an exceptional one-fertile-locule species that appears one-seeded.

shared_traits: Look for star-shaped/scalelike hairs; generic gray fuzz or a brown stem is not sufficient.
Check small unisexual flowers, often on a common mixed inflorescence, then inspect the female style branches.
Leaves are usually alternate and simple, but leaf shape, tooth pattern and woody versus annual growth vary by species.
Most have a multi-part capsule; prairie tea has a distinctive effectively one-seeded capsule.
priority: 1. Woody perennial/subshrub base and finely serrulate leaf edges → C. fruticulosus.
2. Female versus male plants and distinct warty capsule → C. texensis.
3. Dark-brown-centered stellate hairs on lower leaf surface; four style tips → C. monanthogynus.
4. Lower surface without dark dots; six style tips → C. lindheimerianus.
5. Woolly robust pair: female sepal curvature, young-hair color, and mature leaf tips → C. lindheimeri vs true C. capitatus.
6. Do not count C. lindheimeri or C. capitatus as target-zone-certified natives until scientific holds are resolved.
study_strategy.warning: CAUTION: C. capitatus and C. lindheimeri have historic synonym/variety confusion. Their learner admission does not certify local nativity; do not reuse a C. capitatus var. lindheimeri specimen as evidence of true C. capitatus.

comparison_cards.title: Prairie tea vs three-seed croton — brown centers and 4 vs 6
comparison_cards.look_here_first: START on the lower surface of several leaves. Prairie tea has DARK-CENTERED star hairs, while three-seed croton lacks that brown-dot look. Then inspect an actual FEMALE flower: 2 bifid styles = FOUR tips in prairie tea; 3 bifid styles = SIX tips in three-seed. Both current image sets teach habit/flowers but DO NOT resolve these microscale counts.

field_matrix.prairie_tea: DARK brown centers make brown speck effect
field_matrix.three_seed: No brown-centered effect at same magnification
field_matrix.strength: Strong IF actual stellate centers can be resolved
Strong, count true female on exact plant

field_matrix.prairie_tea: Functionally ONE fertile seed, follicle-like fruit
Usually low, branched close to ground

comparison_cards.caution: The verified available photography DOES NOT show true dark hair centers or exactly 4/6 female style tips. The old UT voucher file has unverified public reuse rights and is not featured. Need species-exact legal microscope macros, NOT generic Croton images.

comparison_cards.title: Texas croton vs shrubby croton — male vs woody base
comparison_cards.look_here_first: Texas croton is a dioecious annual: male and female on different plants, narrow leaf blades, warty capsule. Shrubby croton has a genuinely persistent woody base and tiny serrations at leaf margins. Existing photos show male stamens and leaves, not diagnostic female fruit/crown.

field_matrix.fruticulosus: Often broader ovate to ovate-lanceolate, MINUTELY serrulate

field_matrix.texensis: Male/female plants separate; female capsules distinctly WARTY
field_matrix.fruticulosus: Monoecious mixed flower racemes; fruit not warty in comparable way

field_matrix.texensis: C. texensis usually narrow and entire
field_matrix.fruticulosus: C. glandulosus can ALSO have serrulate leaves, but lacks a lasting woody crown
field_matrix.strength: Use full plant base; teeth alone are not a species identity

comparison_cards.caution: The showcased Texas photo is MALE flowers only; it cannot show a warty female capsule or prove dioecy alone. Shrubby photo also hides the woody basal trunk. A serrulate ANNUAL Croton glandulosus (comparison-only) is another possible look-alike: woody crown is essential. The new Gaiacoyote CC0 female flower and underside hairs are now physically installed; the true basal crown and individual marginal teeth remain photographic gaps.

comparison_cards.title: Woolly crotons — lindheimeri versus true capitatus
comparison_cards.look_here_first: DO NOT use wool coloration alone. In mature FEMALE flowers C. lindheimeri typically has long straight/slightly INCURVED sepals and acute leaf tips; TRUE C. capitatus long sepals tend to RECURVE outward. Historical C. capitatus var. lindheimeri usually belongs under C. lindheimeri, not proof of capitatus.

field_matrix.strength: Strong with same stage and correct taxon

comparison_cards.caution: Lindheimeri county-native status UNRESOLVED; true capitatus taxon concept/local count UNRESOLVED. NCSU CC0 photo only proves male flower and hairy plant; does not prove final female sepal split. Do not certify nativity.
